introduction_markdown: Multiple choice paper (0730 English Language 1, GCE Advanced Level, June 2024). Duration: one and a half hours. Answer ALL the 50 questions; all questions carry equal marks. Each question has four suggested answers A, B, C and D: choose the one that best answers the question and mark it on the answer sheet with a soft HB pencil (one answer only; more than one mark scores zero for that question). Avoid spending too much time on any one question. Mobile phones are not allowed in the examination room. The paper has three sections: A reading comprehension (questions 1-16, 16 marks), B grammar (questions 17-38, 22 marks) and C vocabulary (questions 39-50, 12 marks).
enonce_intro_markdown: **Multiple choice questions** - choose the one best answer, A, B, C or D.
incertitudes: Paper de 7 pages, scan sans couche texte avec fantômes de recto/verso : texte relu en image, page par page, puis recontrôlé à fort grossissement. Le passage de compréhension (lignes 1 à 70) est recopié en entier, fautes imprimées comprises : « Excluding women ... imply » (ligne 30, accord fautif), « The first for social reasons » (ligne 38), « books.google.cm » dans la source (lu ainsi sur le sujet, probablement « .com »). Les numéros de ligne sont ceux imprimés (tous les cinq) ; la dernière ligne du passage porte l'impression « 70 » alors que le comptage physique des lignes donne 69 (une ligne de décalage dans le dernier paragraphe, sans effet sur les renvois des questions, qui citent L16-17, L21-22, L24, L31-32, L51-52 et L52-53, tous vérifiés).

Le sujet est un papier à 50 questions sans clé ni corrigé : toutes les clés sont établies par raisonnement sur le passage et par les règles de langue. Les points par section sont ceux imprimés (A 16, B 22, C 12 = 50), non modifiés.

Questions 5, 37 et 44 : clé non établie avec certitude, donc ingérées comme questions OUVERTES (auto-évaluation). Q5 : les affirmations ii et iii sont les seules appuyées par le passage, mais aucune option imprimée ne les donne seules ; l'option la plus proche est B (i, ii et iii). Q37 : les options C (deux-points) et D (point-virgule) sont toutes deux correctement ponctuées. Q44 : dash, run et fly sont tous trois courants pour « I must dash / run / fly » (départ pressé).

Clés conservées mais à relire par un enseignant : Q8 (D reformule presque littéralement la citation, la question dit « implies »), Q16 (ton « critical » retenu, ni sarcastique ni humoristique ni appréciatif), Q25 (« know » seule forme compatible avec la phrase, « will know » n'étant pas proposé), Q29 (ordre des adjectifs : C est la moins fautive des quatre, aucune option ne suit parfaitement l'ordre scolaire), Q31 (tag « will you » retenu pour un impératif, « won't you » et « could you » étant des variantes rares), Q38 (B retenue ; les quatre options contiennent « synonymous to » alors que la préposition usuelle est « with »), Q42 (admittance retenue ; admission et entrance restent concevables), Q45 (B retenue ; D dit « no fun », trop fort pour « could be more fun »), Q48 (C retenue, D « together » est proche).

Les numéros 37, 38, 47 sont imprimés sans point ; les consignes qui précèdent plusieurs questions (35-36, 37-38, 39-44, 45-46, 47-48, 49-50) sont recopiées dans l'énoncé de la première question concernée. Q37 et Q38 : le sujet ne donne pas de phrase à corriger, seulement quatre options ; l'énoncé le dit. Q20 : « James ... her sister » (pronoms discordants) est imprimé tel quel.
Aucune figure : le sujet ne contient ni image ni schéma. Les mots soulignés de l'original sont rendus en gras ; les passages en gras du texte (L17-18, L21-22, L24, L31-32, L52-53) sont conservés.

Converties en questions ouvertes par le relecteur (clé ou options discutables) : 5, 37, 44. Q5 : ii et iii sont les seules affirmations appuyées, aucune option ne les donne seules ; Q37 : C (deux-points) et D (point-virgule) sont tous deux corrects ; Q44 : dash, run et fly sont tous courants.

Ligne 66 du passage : « given the chance » suivi d'un signe lu comme un point (une tache le fait ressembler à deux-points) ; transcrit avec un point. Seconde passe faite : chaque page relue en image à fort grossissement et chaque question refaite une deuxième fois indépendamment ; aucune clé n'a changé.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**Passage for questions 1 to 16** (line numbers are printed in square brackets, every fifth line; bold type is as printed)

Despite the fact that humanity possesses the knowledge and the skill to relieve the suffering of the poor, more than
half of the people of the world are living in conditions approaching misery. Their food is inadequate. They are
victims of disease. Their economic life is primitive and stagnant. Their poverty is a handicap and a threat both to
them and to more prosperous areas. As a result, we must embark on a bold new programme for making the
benefits of our scientific advances and industrial progress available for the improvement and growth of  [5]
underdeveloped areas. I believe that we should make available to peace-loving people the benefits of our store of
technical knowledge in order to help them realize their aspirations for a better life.

Among the natural resources which can be called upon in national plans for development, possibly, the most
important is human labour. As the English language suffers from a certain weakness in its ability to describe
groups composed of both male and female members, this is usually described as "manpower". Without a  [10]
productive labour force, including effective leadership and intelligent middle management, no amount of foreign
assistance or of natural wealth can ensure successful development and modernization.

The manpower for development during the next quarter century will come from the world's present population of
infants, children and adolescents. But we have no assurance that they will be equal to the task. Will they have the
health, the education, the skills, the socio-cultural attitudes essential for the responsibilities of development?  [15]

For far too many of them the answer is no. The reason is basic. Children's most critical years, with regard to
physical, intellectual, social and emotional development, are those before they reach five years of age. **During
those critical formative years, they are cared for exclusively by their mothers,** and in many parts of the world,
mothers may not have the capacity to raise superior children. The woman is incapable of doing so by reason of her
poor health, her ignorance and her lack of status and recognition, of social and legal rights, of economic parity of  [20]
independence. As M. Pierre Emeric Mandl of UNICEF has stated, **"She has been educated to submission; she is
not regarded as a separate and complete human being".** How can such a non-person raise a superior child?
The best she can do is to maintain the status quo, and the status quo is not good enough for development.

One essential factor has been overlooked or ignored. **The forgotten factor** is the role of women. Development
will be handicapped as long as women remain second-class citizens, uneducated, without legal or economic status,  [25]
married when they are still practically children, and henceforth producing one baby after another, often only to see
half of them die before they are of school age.

We can enhance development by improving "womanpower", by giving women the opportunity to develop
themselves. This is especially true as women make up 60% of the world's population. Excluding women from
development endeavours imply that all development effort is hinged on only about 40% of the world's population.  [30]
With this tendency, development cannot progress to meet the needs of society. **Statistics show that the average
family size increases in an inverse ratio to the mother's years of education;** lowest among college graduates
and highest among those with only primary school training or no education.

Malnutrition is most frequent in large families, and increases in frequency with each additional sibling. Birth order
is important too. In a study conducted in India by Dr. Gopalan, malnutrition among the first three children of a  [35]
family was about half as prevalent as among those with a birth order from four to six. Both illegitimacy and
prematurity are more frequent among school dropouts than among girls who complete their education. Both
illegitimacy and prematurity have an adverse effect on the health and development of the child. The first for social
reasons - the lack of a stable environment, and the second, primarily because of the reduced resistance to disease
and infection of the premature infant.  [40]

In recent years, much attention has been given to the relationship between early malnutrition and retarded mental
development. Dr. Mark Hegsted of Harvard School of Public Health and Dr. Michael Latham of Cornell
University have both cautioned against the over-simplification of assuming that malnutrition is the sole, or
principal cause of retardation, or that it can be avoided or mitigated by improved nutrition. However, many of the
other factors in its etiology, such as poor child care and hygiene and the lack of social and emotional stimulus,  [45]
also do relate to the intelligence and education of the mother.

The principle seems to establish that an educated mother has healthier and more intelligent children, and that this
is related to the fact that she has fewer children. The tendency of educated, upper class mothers to have fewer
children operates even without access to contraceptive services, as was noted in Western Europe before the turn of
the century.  [50]

If we examine the opportunities for education of girls or women in less developed countries, we usually find a
**dismal picture.** In some countries, the ratio of boys to girls in secondary schools is more than 7:1. **What happens
to the girls?** Often, they are kept at home to look after younger siblings and to perform a variety of domestic
chores. Their education is not perceived as in any way equal in importance to that of boys. When a non-literate or
barely literate girl reaches adolescence, she has little or no qualification for employment even if her community  [55]
provides any opportunity for the employment of women. The solution is to get her married as soon as possible
with the inevitable result that she produces children, "too soon, too late and too often". With no formal education,
she is hardly aware that there is any alternative. In a study made in Thailand, it was noted that the literate woman
marries later and ceases childbearing earlier than her non-literate counterpart. But the latter is so chained to her
household by the necessities of gathering fuel, preparing food and tending children that she is very difficult to  [60]
reach, even if health services, nutrition education, maternal and child health centres are available in her
community. She does not understand what they are intended to do.

For the world to experience a change of this pattern, there is great need to have a complete overhaul of the
mindset and negative stereotypes towards the woman and the girl child. Women must be seen as human beings
created in the image and likeness of God with tremendous potential to develop and make society forge ahead if  [65]
given the chance. They need quality education and exposure which empower them and help develop their talents
for the enhancement of their families and the society at large. To reverse the situation of misery and acute
impoverishment experienced in many parts of the world as a result of under development and unequal distribution
of wealth, all hands must be put on deck in order to promote the education and exposure of women.  [70]

*(Adapted from Margot Higgins: War on Hunger from books.google.cm)*

**SECTION A - READING COMPREHENSION (16 marks).** Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions below it. Choose the best answer for each question from the alternatives A, B, C or D.

1. The writer's reason for thinking that technological knowledge should be made available for the underdeveloped areas is because \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The reason (the purpose) is stated in lines 6-7: the writer believes the benefits of our store of technical knowledge should be made available "in order to help them realize their aspirations for a better life". Option B restates exactly this. A (humanity possesses the knowledge) is only the concession introduced by "Despite the fact that" in line 1: it says that the means exist, not why they should be shared. C and D (inadequate food, poverty as a handicap) describe the problem, not the writer's reason for the remedy.

**Answer: B.**

choix.texte: humanity possesses the knowledge and skill to relieve the poor
they need it to realize their better life aspirations

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 1 to 16 above)

2. According to the author, human labour is \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Lines 8-9: "Among the natural resources which can be called upon in national plans for development, possibly, the most important is human labour." Human labour is therefore one of the natural resources, and possibly the most important one. B and D confuse the resource with the plans in which it is used. C is wrong because "Among the natural resources" shows that it is not the only one.

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: one of the national plans for development
the only resource which can be called upon by the nation

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 1 to 16 above)

3. "*Manpower*" as used in line 13 is a \_\_\_\_\_\_ word.
questions.corrige_markdown:
"Manpower" is formed by joining two free words, *man* and *power*, into one word with a new meaning: this is a compound word. A simple word has a single root with no affix; a complex word (in word formation) is a root with an affix (for example *happiness*). "Compressed" is not a word-formation term.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 1 to 16 above)

4. \_\_\_\_\_\_ not a prerequisite for successful development and modernization.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Lines 10-12: "Without a productive labour force, including effective leadership and intelligent middle management, no amount of foreign assistance or of natural wealth can ensure successful development and modernization." The labour force, leadership and middle management are the indispensable conditions; foreign assistance and natural wealth alone cannot ensure development, so they are the ones that are not prerequisites. The plural subject in D also takes "are", which fits the blank.

**Answer: D.**

choix.texte: Foreign assistance and natural wealth are

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 1 to 16 above)

5. The writer fears that the development of the next quarter century may be interfered with because:

i. the agents of development may remain as infants, children and adolescents

ii. the agents of development may lack health and education

iii. the agents of development may lack the skills and socio-cultural attitudes essential for development

iv. the agents of development may not receive foreign assistance

*Options as printed:* A) i and iii only   B) i, ii and iii only   C) ii, iii, and iv only   D) iii and iv only
questions.corrige_markdown:
Lines 13-15: the manpower for the next quarter century will come from today's infants, children and adolescents, and "we have no assurance that they will be equal to the task. Will they have the health, the education, the skills, the socio-cultural attitudes essential for the responsibilities of development?" So statements ii (health and education) and iii (skills and attitudes) are the writer's fears. Statement iv is not a fear expressed in the passage (foreign assistance is mentioned only in lines 11-12, as something that cannot replace a productive labour force). Statement i is only loosely supported: the future agents are today's children, but the writer does not fear that they will "remain" children. The exact set (ii and iii only) is not offered; the closest printed option is B (i, ii and iii only).

**Intended answer: B (i, ii and iii only).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 1 to 16 above)

6. In its immediate context, the statement "*During those critical formative years, they are cared for exclusively by their mother.*" (L16-17) means \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
In context (lines 16-19) the first five years are the most critical years of a child's development, and during them the child is looked after only by the mother, whose capacity (health, knowledge, status) therefore decides the child's development. The nearest meaning is that the mother is the only influence and model the child has at that age (B). A and C add details (breast milk, single motherhood) that the passage never states; D contradicts the passage, which says these years are the most critical.

**Answer: B.**

choix.texte: children live on their mother's breast milk for five years
the mother is the child's only role model at that age
the mothers live as single mothers for five years
mothers make those first five years less critical

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 1 to 16 above)

7. We deduce from paragraph four that superior children can only be raised when \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Paragraph four (lines 16-23) says that the mother cannot raise superior children because of her poor health, her ignorance and "her lack of status and recognition, of social and legal rights"; the best she can do is to maintain the status quo, which is "not good enough for development". By implication, superior children can be raised only when her status is fully recognised (D). A and B are not mentioned in the paragraph, and C is the opposite of what the writer wants.

**Answer: D.**

choix.texte: the society has the wealth to educate them
the status of the woman is fully recognised

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 1 to 16 above)

8. "*She has been educated to submission, she is not regarded as a separate and complete human being*" (L21-22) This statement implies that \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The quotation says that the woman is not regarded as a separate and complete human being; this is what the statement implies about her position in society, and option D is the only one that follows from it. A (suits her class) and B (illiterate) are never suggested, and C changes the point: the writer is not judging the content of her education but the lack of recognition of her personhood. Option D is a close restatement of the quotation, which is what makes the question easy.

**Answer: D.**

choix.texte: the woman's education suits her class
the woman is not regarded as a separate human being

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 1 to 16 above)

9. According to the passage, the woman is considered the "*forgotten factor*" (L24) in relation to \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Lines 24-25: "One essential factor has been overlooked or ignored. The forgotten factor is the role of women. Development will be handicapped as long as women remain second-class citizens..." The whole passage is about development, so the woman is the forgotten factor in developmental issues (A). The economy, marital issues and education are only aspects of the larger question of development.

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: the role of the woman in developmental issues
the role of the woman in the economy
the role of the woman in marital issues
the role of the woman in educational issues

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 1 to 16 above)

10. From the statement "*Statistics show that the average family size increases in an inverse ratio to the mother's years of education*" (L31-32), we understand that \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
An inverse ratio means that when one quantity rises the other falls. Family size rises when the mother's years of education fall, so the more education the mother has, the smaller the family. The next lines confirm it: family size is "lowest among college graduates and highest among those with only primary school training or no education". A and C state a direct relationship, D is irrelevant.

**Answer: B.**

choix.texte: the higher the mother's education, the bigger the family size
the higher the mother's education, the smaller the family size
the lower the mother's education, the smaller the family size
the lower the mother's education, the higher training she gets for her children

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 1 to 16 above)

11. Mental retardation is caused by all of the following except \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Lines 44-46 list the other factors that relate to retardation: "poor child care and hygiene and the lack of social and emotional stimulus". The reduced resistance to disease and infection (lines 39-40) is mentioned in a different context, as the reason why prematurity harms the physical health of the infant, not as a cause of mental retardation. So D is the exception. The question is of the "except" type: three options are in the passage's list, one is not.

**Answer: D.**

choix.texte: reduced resistance to disease and infection

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 1 to 16 above)

12. The expression "*a dismal picture*" (L51-52) means \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
"Dismal" means gloomy, depressing, and "picture" is used figuratively for the overall situation. The paragraph goes on to describe girls kept at home, ratios of boys to girls of 7:1 and women without qualifications: a sad, bleak situation (C). A and B take "picture" literally as a show; D takes it as physical appearance, which is not what the writer describes.

**Answer: C.**
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 1 to 16 above)

13. The question "*what happens to the girls?*" (L52-53) is a \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The writer does not ask the question to obtain information: it is asked for effect and answered at once ("Often, they are kept at home..."). That is a rhetorical question. A tag question is a short question added to a statement ("isn't it?"); a yes/no question expects "yes" or "no" and a "what" question does not; a multiple choice question offers options.

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level English - figures of speech

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 1 to 16 above)

14. The passage emphasizes that in less developed countries \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The passage describes the unequal treatment of girls (lines 51-62) and ends with the call for "quality education and exposure" for women and for a change of the mindset (lines 63-70). The message is that girls and boys must be given equal educational opportunities (D). A is the mistaken view that the writer criticises, B contradicts the passage (the non-literate woman is the one who is disadvantaged), and C is never said.

**Answer: D.**

choix.texte: the education of girls is not important
the non-literate woman has some advantages because she has more children
a literate female is a threat to the male in employment
there is a need to give both sexes equal opportunities in education

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 1 to 16 above)

15. The writer of this passage is most likely a \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The writer argues from beginning to end for the education, the legal and economic status and the recognition of women ("all hands must be put on deck in order to promote the education and exposure of women"). Someone who defends the rights and opportunities of women is a feminist. A misogynist hates or despises women, which is the opposite; a historian would narrate the past; a moralist would stress right and wrong conduct rather than the status of women.

**Answer: C.**
themes: A Level English - tone and attitude

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 1 to 16 above)

16. The general tone of this passage is \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The passage is serious and concerned. It criticises the neglect of women's education and status ("second-class citizens", "a dismal picture", "negative stereotypes") and the attitudes that keep women down, and it calls for change. The tone is therefore critical (D). It is neither sarcastic nor humorous, and nothing in it is appreciative of the present situation.

**Answer: D.**
themes: A Level English - tone and attitude

questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION B - GRAMMAR (22 marks).** Choose the alternative A, B, C or D that best completes each sentence below.

17. The man **who lives upstairs** is of very good conduct. The underlined clause is an example of a/an \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
"Who lives upstairs" is introduced by the relative pronoun *who* and identifies which man is meant: without it, "the man" would not be specific. It is written without commas, so it is a defining (restrictive) relative clause. A non-defining clause only adds extra information and is set off by commas. An adverbial clause would be introduced by a conjunction of time, reason and so on. D is true but less precise than C, and the question asks for the best description.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 18. We enjoy sitting on the \_\_\_\_\_\_ seat.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The usual order of adjectives is opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material. Here: *fantastic* (opinion), *soft* (physical quality), *grey* (colour), *leather* (material). So "fantastic soft grey leather seat" (D). In C the colour comes before the physical quality; A and B put the opinion adjective in the wrong place.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 19. She fell from the \_\_\_\_\_\_ floor of the building.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The correct word meaning "highest" is *topmost* (or *uppermost*). Of the options only D is a real word, here written with a hyphen. "Upper most" is written as two words, and "most up" and "most upper" are not English forms.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 20. James is tired of **writing** letters to her sister because she never replies. The underlined word functions in the sentence as a/an \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
"Writing" comes after the preposition *of* and is the head of the noun phrase "writing letters to her sister" (it takes the object *letters*): a verb form used as a noun is a gerund. A participle would work as an adjective ("the writing man") or form part of a verb phrase ("is writing"). The mismatch of pronouns in the printed sentence ("James ... her sister") does not change the analysis.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 21. Peter bought a car after he had completed his studies. This is an example of a \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The sentence has one main clause ("Peter bought a car") and one subordinate clause ("after he had completed his studies"), introduced by the subordinating conjunction *after*. One main clause plus one or more subordinate clauses make a complex sentence. A compound sentence joins two main clauses (with *and*, *but*); a compound-complex sentence has at least two main clauses and a subordinate clause.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 22. Jack promised to help me but later \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
To *back out* is to withdraw from a promise, an agreement or a commitment, which is exactly what Jack did. *Back away* is to move physically away, *back off* is to retreat or stop interfering, and *back up* is to support or to make a copy.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 23. Remember this matter is strictly \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
After a preposition (*between*) the pronouns must be in the object case: *me*, not *I*. Both "between you and me" and "between me and you" are grammatical, but only C is the established idiom ("strictly between you and me"), and the polite order puts the other person first. A and B use the subject pronoun *I*, which is wrong after a preposition.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 24. You have failed twice. You \_\_\_\_\_\_ working harder or you won't succeed in the course.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The fixed expression for strong advice is *had better* followed by the bare infinitive: "You had better start working harder". B, C and D break the pattern (*better* without *had*, *to* after *had better*, past tense after *had better*).

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 25. If you watch the movie, you \_\_\_\_\_\_ how it ends.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The condition ("If you watch the movie") is in the present simple, so the result clause uses the present (a general truth, the zero conditional: if you watch it, you know how it ends) or *will* + infinitive. Of the options only "know" fits the sequence of tenses. B (past) and C (third conditional result) belong to other conditionals; D (future perfect) does not express a result that follows the watching.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 26. Many investors are limiting the expansion of their businesses in our region and other areas \_\_\_\_\_\_ violent attacks.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Areas that often suffer violent attacks are said to be *prone to* them, which explains why investors limit expansion. "Safe from" gives the opposite meaning (no reason to limit expansion), "close to" does not express a tendency, and "hostile to" would mean that the areas themselves are unfriendly to attacks.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 27. There is \_\_\_\_\_\_ oil in the cup which you could use in cooking the meal.
questions.corrige_markdown:
*Oil* is uncountable, so the quantifier must be *a little* (some, a small but useful amount), which fits "which you could use". *Little* without the article means "hardly any" and contradicts the idea that you can use it. *Small* and *a small* cannot modify an uncountable noun in this way.

**Answer: C.**
themes: A Level English - articles and determiners

questions.enonce_markdown: 28. Young children are always advised to hang \_\_\_\_\_\_ to their dreams.
questions.corrige_markdown:
To *hang on to* something is to hold on to it, to keep it. The meaning here is that children should not give up their dreams. *Hang up* (end a call, put on a hook), *hang out* (spend time) and *hang forth* do not take "to their dreams".

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 29. My brother bought a \_\_\_\_\_\_ motorbike.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Only C is a natural, grammatical string: *brand-new* (an intensified form of *new*) comes first, followed by *modern*, *big*, the colour *black* and the origin *Chinese*, with colour and origin close to the noun as the usual order requires. In A, *brand-new* is wrongly put after the origin. In B, "new brand" is not a valid modifier (the compound is *brand-new*). In D the order is reversed. C is the best of four imperfect orders; none follows the textbook order perfectly (size would normally precede age).

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: big modern black Chinese new brand
black Chinese new brand modern big

questions.enonce_markdown: 30. \_\_\_\_\_\_ have got the required skills needed for the assignment.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The compound is the subject of "have got", so both pronouns must be in the subject case (*he*, *I*). The polite order is the other person first, then *I*: "He and I". A and B contain object pronouns (*me*, *him*) in subject position; C has the object pronoun *him* and puts *I* first.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 31. Think before you speak, \_\_\_\_\_\_?
questions.corrige_markdown:
A question tag after an imperative is normally *will you?* (a request or command). "Won't you" is an invitation ("Have a seat, won't you?"), "wouldn't you" asks about a hypothetical situation and "could you" is a polite request that does not fit a warning. The standard textbook tag for a plain imperative is *will you*.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 32. I didn't want to take part in the discussions. \_\_\_\_\_\_, I walked out.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The second sentence gives what the speaker did in place of taking part: "Instead, I walked out". "On the contrary" contradicts a statement or opinion; "All the same" (nevertheless) would make the walking out surprising given the first sentence; "Similarly" introduces a parallel idea.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 33. Mr Mathew, **the control agent**, became the first foreigner to be honoured. The underlined section of the sentence can be best described as a/an \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
"The control agent" is a noun phrase placed next to the noun "Mr Mathew" to rename and identify him, set off by commas: that is an appositive. It has no verb (so not a clause), no preposition (so not a prepositional phrase), and it is correctly attached to its noun (so not a dangling modifier).

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 34. You **ought** to work harder for the upcoming examination. Ought is used as a/an \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
*Ought to* is a modal verb (a modal auxiliary of obligation and advice, like *should*). It is not a particle, a command (an imperative is a sentence type, not a word class) or an adverbial.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
For questions 35 and 36, choose from the alternatives A, B, C or D the sentence that is correctly reported.

35. The patient asked the doctor, "*Is there time to do it now?*"
questions.corrige_markdown:
A yes/no question is reported with *whether* or *if*, the verb moves to statement order and back-shifts (*is* becomes *was*), and *now* becomes *then*. So: "asked the doctor whether there was time to do it then". A turns the question into a statement with a different meaning. B changes "there was time" to "it was time", which changes the meaning. D keeps the present tense and "now" and drops "it".

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: The patient wanted the doctor to know it was time to do it.
The patient asked the doctor whether it was time to do it then.
The patient asked the doctor whether there was time to do it then
The patient asked the doctor if there is time to do now.

questions.enonce_markdown: 36. "*It rained yesterday and most of last week,*" said Ralph.
questions.corrige_markdown:
In reported speech after a past reporting verb, the past simple becomes the past perfect (*had rained*), *yesterday* becomes *the day before* (or *the previous day*) and *last week* becomes *the previous week* (or *the week before*). A does all three. B keeps *yesterday*; C keeps the simple past; D changes the meaning ("the week that followed").

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: Ralph said that it had rained the day before and most of the previous week
Ralph said that it had rained yesterday and most of that week
Ralph said that it rained the previous day and most of the week before
Ralph said that it had rained the previous day and the week that followed

questions.enonce_markdown:
For questions 37 and 38, choose from the alternatives A, B, C or D the sentence that is correctly punctuated.

37. (No stem is printed: choose the sentence that is correctly punctuated.)

*Options as printed:* A) You did very well in the role play, you spoke clearly and constructed some complex sentences.   B) You did very well, in the role play you spoke clearly and constructed some complex sentences.   C) You did very well in the role play: you spoke clearly and constructed some complex sentences.   D) You did very well in the role play; you spoke clearly and constructed some complex sentences.
questions.corrige_markdown:
A joins two independent clauses with a comma only (a comma splice), and B does the same after misplacing the comma. Both C and D are correct: a colon introduces an explanation of the first clause, and a semicolon links two closely related independent clauses. Because C and D are both defensible, the key is not certain.

**Intended answer: C or D (colon or semicolon after "role play").**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level English - spelling and punctuation

questions.enonce_markdown: 38. (No stem is printed: choose the sentence that is correctly punctuated.)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Words that are talked about as words are put in quotation marks, with no comma between "word" and the quoted term: The word "dictation" is... (B). A has a comma and no quotation marks; C has a misplaced comma after *dictation*; D has an unnecessary comma after *word*. All four share the phrase "synonymous to" (the standard preposition is *with*), which does not help choose between them.

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level English - spelling and punctuation

choix.texte: The word, dictation is synonymous to old fashion.
The word "dictation" is synonymous to "old fashion".
The word dictation, is synonymous to old fashion.
The word, "dictation" is synonymous to "old fashion".

questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION C - VOCABULARY (12 marks).**

For questions 39-44, choose the alternative A, B, C or D that best completes the sentence.

39. The explanation to his action was simply incomprehens\_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The adjective is *incomprehensible* (the root *comprehend* gives *comprehensible*, with the suffix *-ible*, as in *responsible*). *Incomprehensiveness* is a noun with another meaning, *incomprehensable* is a misspelling, and *incomprehensive* means not covering everything.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 40. Cat is to mew as \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The analogy pairs an animal with the sound it makes: a cat mews, a cricket chirps. The other pairs are wrong: a horse neighs (a sheep or goat bleats), a goat bleats (a frog croaks) and an elephant trumpets (a horse neighs).

**Answer: A.**
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: 41. He was told to get a decent \_\_\_\_\_\_ for the guests.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The correct spelling has a double *c* and a double *m*: accommodation. The other options each miss one doubled letter.

**Answer: D.**
themes: A Level English - spelling and punctuation

questions.enonce_markdown: 42. Jake's good looks was the reason for his \_\_\_\_\_\_ into the Managing Director's office.
questions.corrige_markdown:
*Admittance* is the act of being allowed to enter a place, and is the word used with *into* a room or building ("No admittance"). *Admission* is more usual for institutions, events and confessions (admission to a school, admission fee), *access* is followed by *to* and means the right or means of approach, and *entrance* is the act of coming in or the door itself. The best fit is A, although *admission* and *entrance* are not impossible.

**Answer: A.**
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: 43. The victims of the accident were bleeding \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The collocation for heavy bleeding is *bleeding profusely* (in large quantity). "Badly" is possible in everyday speech but "profusely" is the precise word; "profoundly" and "deeply" describe feelings or depth (profoundly moved, deeply wounded), not quantity of blood.

**Answer: C.**
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown:
44. Peter is in a hurry. This implies that he must \_\_\_\_\_\_ now.

*Options as printed:* A) dash   B) skip   C) run   D) fly
questions.corrige_markdown:
A person in a hurry who has to leave must *dash* (rush quickly), as in "I must dash". *Skip* means to leave out or to move lightly. *Run* and *fly* can also be used informally for leaving in a hurry ("I must run", "I must fly"), so the key is not certain.

**Intended answer: A (dash).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown:
For questions 45 and 46, choose the alternative A, B, C or D that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence given.

45. If he were here it could be more fun.
questions.corrige_markdown:
"If he were here" is a present unreal condition: he is not here, and the occasion would be more fun if he were. B says exactly that: he is absent and the occasion lacks fun. A adds a trait (good humour) not in the sentence; C says he was expected, which is not stated; D says there was "no fun", which exaggerates "could be more fun" and uses the past. B is the best option although it also states that he "did not show up".

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

choix.texte: We missed his good humoured nature at the occasion.
He did not show up and so the occasion lacked much fun.
He was expected but did not show up.
There was no fun because he was not present.

questions.enonce_markdown: 46. How does he come into the picture?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The idiom "to come into the picture" means to become involved in a situation, so the question asks what his role in the affair is (A). The other options take "picture" literally or change the subject.

**Answer: A.**
themes: A Level English - idioms and proverbs

choix.texte: What is his part in this affair?
Why was he included in the picture?
How do we include him into the scene?
When does he appear on the scene?

questions.enonce_markdown:
For questions 47 and 48, choose the best answer from the alternatives A, B, C or D that has the same meaning as the underlined expressions.

47. The balanced sheet of our social group at the end of this year shows that we **broke even**.
questions.corrige_markdown:
To *break even* is to end with neither profit nor loss: income equals expenditure. A is the opposite of a loss, C and D mean the group is in debt or losing money.

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level English - idioms and proverbs

questions.enonce_markdown: 48. During the last Mount Cameroon Race of Hope, the sprinters were running **neck and neck**.
questions.corrige_markdown:
*Neck and neck* is a racing idiom (from horse racing) meaning side by side, level with each other, with no one ahead. C expresses this. D (together) is close but loses the idea of competition and of an equal position in a race; A and B are about speed.

**Answer: C.**
themes: A Level English - idioms and proverbs

questions.enonce_markdown:
For questions 49 and 50, choose the best answer from the alternatives A, B, C and D that is opposite in meaning to the underlined word.

49. Francis Ngannou is an **amateur** wrestler.
questions.corrige_markdown:
An amateur does something for pleasure, without payment; the opposite is a professional. "Good", "bad" and "skilful" describe quality, and an amateur can be skilful.

**Answer: C.**
themes: A Level English - synonyms and antonyms

questions.enonce_markdown: 50. The author's write-up contained a **plethora** of details.
questions.corrige_markdown:
*Plethora* means an excessive amount, too much. Its opposite is a shortage (a lack). *Variety* and *complexity* are not about quantity, and *simplicity* is the opposite of complexity, not of abundance.

**Answer: D.**
themes: A Level English - synonyms and antonyms
